threads.old: Glaucon is the unnamed companion at the dialogue's opening who asks Apollodorus to repeat the conversation about love that was held at Agathon's symposium. He serves as the occasion for Apollodorus's narration.
threads.new: Glaucon is the acquaintance who, two days before the dialogue opens, stopped Apollodorus on the road into Athens to ask about the speeches on love at Agathon's party. He had heard only a vague account, passed on from Phoenix, and assumed the party was recent; Apollodorus told him it had happened long ago, when they were boys, and that his own source was Aristodemus. They went over the story as they walked, which is why Apollodorus is ready to tell it again to the unnamed companion who asks him now.
threads.reason: The restored opening (candidate 1.0-1.8) shows that Glaucon and the companion are different people: Glaucon questioned Apollodorus two days earlier; the companion who asks now is unnamed. The current text says Glaucon IS the unnamed companion.

onboardingOptional.old: And now I will tell you the reason why, and what the original nature of man was, and the great change which was made in him. The sexes were not two as they are now, but originally three in number; there was man, woman, and the union of the two, having a name corresponding to this double nature, which had once a real existence, but is now lost, though a word of ill omen.
onboardingOptional.new: In the first place, let me treat of the nature of man and what has happened to it; for the original human nature was not like the present, but different. The sexes were not two as they are now, but originally three in number; there was man, woman, and the union of the two, having a name corresponding to this double nature, which had once a real existence, but is now lost, and the word 'Androgynous' is only preserved as a term of reproach.
